title: I Said No to Jimmy Iovine
author: The Best Leadership Newsletter
summary: The author tells the story of being invited to Jimmy Iovine's house at 27 and never going, because he feared being exposed as a fraud and believed accepting help meant admitting he was not good enough. He explains that he spent the first fifteen years of his career trying to be an expert at everything alone, treating requests for help as a weakness. After a recent college panel, a student reached out on LinkedIn, putting the author on the other side of the door he once avoided. He now makes a living as a coach helping leaders who feel stuck, offering the outside perspective he wishes he had received. The takeaway is a direct question about where the reader needs help and a push to walk through the door when someone opens it. The piece ends with a promotion for a paid leadership program.
points: The author skipped a career-changing invitation because fear of being exposed disguised itself as busyness and bad timing.
He equated asking for help with inadequacy, a belief that kept him working alone for fifteen years.
Nobody is an expert at everything and nobody builds anything meaningful alone, so asking for help signals self-awareness rather than weakness.
Seeing a student reach out after a panel showed him that people genuinely want to help those who ask.
Part of the cost of avoidance is unknowable, because you never learn what the missed conversation would have changed.
quotes: I was scared I’d walk into Jimmy Iovine’s house, sit across from him, and in a few minutes he’d realize he’d made a huge mistake.
What’s an even harder peach pit for me to swallow is my belief that accepting his help meant admitting that I needed help. And I thought needing help meant I wasn’t good enough to do it myself.
I spent the first 15 years of my career believing I was supposed to be an expert at everything, without anybody else’s help.
Nobody is an expert at everything. Nobody builds anything meaningful by themselves.
Because here’s the thing I didn’t understand when I was younger: People actually want to help you.
I can help you see the thing you can’t see because you’re standing too close to it.

Because asking for help doesn’t mean you’re incapable of doing it yourself. It doesn’t mean you’re an idiot. Sometimes it just means you’re smart enough to realize that you don’t have all the answers.
